transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-04 15:00 UTC | Duration: 46 minutes | Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), James Li (Lumen Head of ML), Maria Ortiz (Infra), Ben Carter (CTO)

Summary: cost/unit economics deep dive — customer wants comparison hosted vs dedicated vs private for a retrieval-augmented chat product. Focus on per-token math, batching/caching levers, latency SLOs, and budget constraints; request for benchmark pilot and security docs.

[00:00] Alex: Hey everybody, thanks for joining. quick intro, i'm alex from redwood, with priya who is our systems engineer, and we wanted to run through cost economics and make sure we model the right assumptions for your use case.
[00:12] James: yeah thanks alex, i'm james, we run the ml stack at lumen. main thing for us is we need to understand unit cost for inference — per token — and how batching / kv cache will affect that. our budget for inference is roughly $12k a month to start and we need to see if hosted can fit or we need dedicated.
[00:29] Priya: cool, can you share high level numbers — like average prompt length, avg generated tokens, and concurrency? even ballpark helps.
[00:37] James: for our chat assistant, avg prompt is 300 tokens, generation around 150 tokens, concurrency peaks at 40 rps during market open windows but average more like 8 simultaneous sessions. latency target is sub 600ms p50 for user-facing flows.
[00:53] Ben: and we do sensitive doc retrieval so data residency / encryption matters, we may push to private later but want to start with hosted if cost is right.
[01:02] Alex: good — so two levers we usually call out: batching (bigger batch = lower per-token compute cost) and prefix/KV caching (avoid recomputing encoder/prefix or repeated context). also model choice and quantization matter a lot. priya, do you want to walk through a simple per-token example?
[01:15] Priya: sure. so baseline: hosted per token list price varies by model but for an open-llm style model we typically show $0.00006 to $0.00012 per generated token for smaller models, and up to $0.0004 for larger dense models. that's public pricing bands; for dedicated reserved capacity the marginal cost per token can drop substantially because you control GPU amortization — often by 2–5x depending on utilization and model.
[01:40] Maria: when you say batching, how big of a delta are we talking? our peak windows are spiky so i'm worried about averaging.
[01:47] Priya: good question — throughput scales with batch size and the GPU type. for example, on an A100-like instance with an optimized runtime, going from batch size 1 to batch 8 can reduce per-token GPU time by ~2.2x; from 1 to 32 maybe 3–4x but latency tail increases. for interactive latency SLOs you tend to cap batching to keep p95 sane. with our smart batching you can target a p50 latency and still get batching wins.
[02:15] James: and kv cache? we've got a lot of repeated retrieval tokens. how does that reduce cost?
[02:19] Priya: KV cache — prefix caching — avoids recomputing earlier attention states for the same context across requests. for retrieval-augmented flows where you pull the same doc snippets, you can see token savings of 20–60% on generation compute, depending on overlap. caveats: cache hit rate matters and you need sticky routing or a shared KV cache in dedicated/private to maximize hits.
[02:39] Ben: ok good, interested in quantization as well — if we go 4-bit quantized models how does quality vs cost trade look?
[02:45] Priya: 4-bit quantization (QLoRA-style or newer dynamic quant) usually reduces memory footprints and increases throughput. In practice, moving from fp16 to 4-bit can yield 1.8–2.5x throughput improvement depending on kernel support, which again reduces per-token cost. quality regressions exist but for many retrieval augmented QA workloads they are acceptable; we recommend running evals against your prompt set.
[03:07] Alex: just adding — for hosted we provide model variants with verified perf profiles. for Dedicated you can pin a quantized build and get consistent throughput; for Private you'll have more control over GPU selection.
[03:15] James: what's the break-even for dedicated? ie, at what usage does dedicated become cheaper than hosted?
[03:20] Priya: depends on utilization and term. rough rule: if you have sustained 6–8k tokens/sec average sustained, or heavy concurrency that fills reserved GPUs, dedicated usually becomes more economical. but that's a high-level. for your $12k/month, if you average low tens of thousands tokens/min you're probably still in hosted economics unless you can commit to a monthly reserved capacity.
[03:43] Maria: could you walk through a toy cost model? like per-month math for our numbers?
[03:46] Alex: yes — quick back-of-envelope. assume avg total tokens per request = 450 (300 prompt + 150 gen). at 8 concurrent sessions, say 8 rps sustained = 8 * 60 * 60 * 24 * 30 ~ 20.7M requests/month — that's way too big; so better to use expected rps. let's use your actual average: you said avg concurrency 8 but rps per user maybe 0.1? James, can you clarify daily active sessions?
[04:12] James: right yeah sorry, concurrency 8 is simultaneous open sessions but each session requests maybe 0.05 rps average overall — so let's say 1k requests/min total which is 43.2M requests/month — ok math is fuzzy. our product team gave us an estimate of 6M generated tokens/month to start.
[04:28] Priya: ok 6M generated tokens: if hosted per generated token is $0.00012 that's $720/month just for generation tokens; include prompt tokens (assume prompts billed too) — if prompts are ~12M tokens/month at same rate that's $1,440; so total ~$2,160/month. those are naive numbers. with batching and caching we can lower compute used and hosted volume discounts and reserved capacity can push that lower.
[04:52] Ben: that seems within the $12k budget. but we also have embeddings and re-ranking costs, and peaky windows.
[05:00] Priya: embeddings cost different units, we typically price per-embedding unit; but for initial model we can add that to the spreadsheet. important: network and infra egress for Private or VPC also adds cost.
[05:11] James: in terms of SLOs, if we want p50 300–400ms and p95 < 900ms, is hosted realistic?
[05:18] Priya: yes for smaller models and with prefix caching; for larger models you may see p50 higher. hosted runs in multiple regions so you can route to nearest; Dedicated can guarantee lower variance since you own GPU pool. we can run a 48-hour benchmark of your prompt set on hosted at no charge to measure p50/p95.
[05:34] Alex: just to highlight other cost levers — autoscaling/burst pools can handle peaks without you committing to large reserved capacity; we also expose batching and cache config knobs. our Optimize product can recommend batch sizes and quantization slots to hit target CPA.
[05:49] Maria: how do you handle cache continuity across replicas? if we autoscale up/down will we lose KV cache and impact hit rates?
[05:56] Priya: good question. in hosted we shard KV caches and have a cache warming strategy; for Dedicated/Private you can enable shared KV cache layer which preserves hits across replicas. there can be a warm-up penalty when scaling. we typically recommend a small hot pool for low-latency traffic.
[06:12] James: security checklist — SOC2, SAML SSO, KMS integration, audit logs — do you provide those docs?
[06:18] Priya: yes we'll share SOC2 reports, SSO/SAML guides, and our KMS integration notes. for private/on-prem we support customer-managed KMS/HSM and full audit logs.
[06:27] Ben: any gotchas on data retention or PII? we need to ensure prompt content isn't retained for more than X days and logs are encrypted at rest.
[06:33] Alex: we offer configurable retention windows, and for enterprise customers we can set zero retention or customer-side encryption keys. we'll include that in the security pack.
[06:42] James: ok hypotheticals — if we want to hit $0.00004 per gen token, is that realistic?
[06:47] Priya: $0.00004 is in the ballpark of what large reserved fleets with heavy batching and quantized models achieve — usually 3–5x reduction vs on-demand hosted. requires high utilization, model selection (quantized, efficient arch), and aggressive batching which may increase tail latency. but for background or async jobs it's common.
[07:06] Alex: we can show modeled scenarios in the spreadsheet: hosted on-demand, hosted with commit discounts, Dedicated reserved (monthly commit), and Private (CAPEX + ops).
[07:15] Maria: for the pilot, we'd like to run the hosted benchmark first then evaluate a Dedicated reserved quote if the numbers justify.
[07:21] James: timeline — I'm thinking 2–3 week pilot, then finance review and decision within 6–8 weeks.
[07:27] Alex: that works. we'll start by capturing your canonical prompt set and expected concurrency profile and run the 48-hour benchmark.
[07:33] Priya: i'll run perf captures and include raw GPU token/sec metrics, expected per-token latency at different batch sizes, and cache hit assumptions.
[07:40] Ben: also include a scenario for embedding re-ranking costs and a worst-case for peak traffic so our infra team can see capex impact.
[07:48] Alex: noted. any other questions?
[07:50] James: one more — do you have any reference customers in finance or with similar workloads?
[07:55] Alex: yes, we can share anonymized case studies — we've worked with a few quant shops and fintech firms running retrieval-augmented agents with similar token profiles. i'll add those links.
[08:04] Maria: ok good. thanks team.
[08:06] Alex: we'll follow up with the pricing spreadsheet and security pack. thanks everyone.

(End of call)
